content: Children aged 1 to 5 years who are enrolled in Medicaid are at a significantly higher risk of having elevated blood lead levels (BLLs). Despite federal requirements for blood lead screening in the Medicaid program, approximately 81% of these children have not undergone a blood lead test. This lack of screening results in many children with elevated BLLs going undiagnosed and untreated, thereby missing critical medical and environmental interventions. To address this issue, the Advisory Committee on Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention (ACCLPP) has outlined specific recommendations for healthcare providers and state agencies. Healthcare providers and health plans are required to perform blood lead screening and provide diagnostic and treatment services for Medicaid-enrolled children, as mandated by federal law. Children with elevated BLLs should be referred for environmental and public health follow-up services. States must revise their policies and programs to ensure compliance with federal Medicaid requirements and to guarantee that children receive the necessary screening and follow-up care. The ACCLPP emphasizes that all children enrolled in Medicaid should be screened for lead exposure at 12 and 24 months of age. If a child has not been previously screened, testing should occur between 36 and 72 months of age. Risk assessment questionnaires are not an acceptable substitute for blood lead tests under Medicaid regulations. Screening at both 1 and 2 years of age is critical, as BLLs tend to peak between 18 and 24 months. Identifying elevated BLLs early can prevent further increases and allow for timely medical and environmental interventions. Children identified with elevated BLLs require comprehensive evaluation and follow-up care, including medical management, environmental investigation, and case management services. These services aim to reduce lead exposure and mitigate the adverse health effects associated with elevated BLLs. Public health and environmental agencies often play a key role in coordinating these follow-up services. The ACCLPP also recommends that states monitor the performance of blood lead screening programs and implement innovative strategies to improve screening rates in areas where traditional methods have been insufficient. States should ensure that Medicaid policies align with federal requirements, support healthcare providers in delivering screening and follow-up services, and provide adequate reimbursement for these services. Additionally, states should develop information systems to track blood lead screening rates and the prevalence of elevated BLLs among Medicaid-enrolled children. New technologies, such as portable blood lead testing devices, offer opportunities to enhance screening services. These devices provide real-time results, allowing for immediate feedback to families and reducing delays in follow-up care. However, their use is currently limited to certified laboratories due to regulatory requirements. Collaboration between Medicaid and public health agencies is essential to explore innovative ways to integrate these technologies into lead poisoning prevention programs. Finally, partnerships between Medicaid agencies and other programs serving children, such as the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) and Head Start, can help increase screening rates and ensure that children receive appropriate services. Public health agencies should review successful models and adapt them to improve blood lead screening performance for Medicaid-enrolled children.
